Hans Egede
häns ā'gê-dê
n. (Hans Egede, 1686–1758, Norwegian Lutheran pastor, missionary to Greenland from 1721, called the apostle of Greenland)
Danish-Norwegian Hans, a form of Johannes; Egede, from a Norwegian farm name.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hans Egede was a Lutheran pastor in the Lofoten islands who became convinced that the Norse colonies planted in Greenland in the tenth century must still exist, cut off from the church for three hundred years, and spent a decade petitioning Copenhagen to let him go to them. He sailed in 1721 with his wife Gertrud and their children. There were no Norse; they had died out. He stayed anyway, among the Inuit, for fifteen years, learning Kalaallisut, translating, and enduring a failed trading company, scurvy and hostility. In 1733 a smallpox epidemic brought by a returning Greenlander killed perhaps two thirds of the population of the district; Egede and his family nursed the dying, and Gertrud died of exhaustion in 1735. He took her body home the next year and spent his last years training missionaries for the work. Mat 9:37 is the field he found. 1Co 15:58 is what held him when the errand failed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an apostle, secondarily, as the first preacher of the gospel in a country; and pestilence, as plague; any contagious disease that is epidemic and mortal.

expand to see more

APOS'TLE, n. The word is also applied to the first preacher of the gospel in any country.

PES'TILENCE, n. Plague, appropriately so called; but in a general sense, any contagious or infectious disease that is epidemic and mortal.

CAT'ECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer in the rudiments of the Christian religion.

Key Scripture

Mat 9:37 — "Then saith he unto his disciples, The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few;"

1Co 15:58 — "Therefore, my beloved brethren, be ye stedfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord."

Jas 1:27 — "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world."

Psa 126:6 — "He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him."

Modern Corruption

He went to Greenland to find a lost Norse church, found none, and stayed fifteen years among the people who were there.

expand to see more

Egede's premise was wrong and his obedience was not. A man who has spent ten years arguing for a mission and arrives to find its object does not exist has every excuse to sail home. He read the situation instead as the field God had actually given him. Mat 9:37 says the harvest is plenteous and the labourers few, and the verse does not add that the harvest must be the one the labourer expected.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The smallpox epidemic is the part that must not be softened. The disease came with European contact, the Egedes were part of that contact, and the mission's most Christlike hour — nursing the dying through a winter until his wife died of it — was spent among people his own civilization had infected. Jas 1:27 defines pure religion as visiting the afflicted, and that winter is what the definition looks like. Psa 126:6 promises the weeping sower his sheaves.

Usage

"“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few” (Mat 9:37) — not the harvest he expected."

"“To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction” (Jas 1:27) — the smallpox winter."

"“He that goeth forth and weepeth, bearing precious seed” (Psa 126:6) — fifteen years of it."
